proposals.relationship: Calloway uses Crosby’s Columbian Exchange to frame colonization as an exchange of organisms and diseases that changed Native capacities for resistance.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2011 interview, displayed version updated2022; specific conceptual resource, not a sole-cause explanation or a dated origin of Calloway’s research. Crosby’s 1972 book remains unread. Calloway’s priority claim about epidemic scholarship is his assessment, not an independently established first.
primary_locators: Five Books, section2 The Columbian Exchange, both answers beginning with the1972 publication and ending with intertribal power balances.

proposals.relationship: Calloway identifies Deloria’s critique of outside experts as a continuing caution for his own practice and accountability to Native communities.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview section3 explicitly includes himself among non-Native researchers made to reconsider their methods. The1969 collection remains unread; this is acknowledged methodological use, not an inference about Indigenous identity.
primary_locators: Five Books, section3 Custer Died for Your Sins, answers on changed scholarly practice, contemporary communities and the caution posed by satirical anthropologists.

proposals.relationship: Calloway draws on White’s account of negotiated Native power and cultural accommodation to unsettle an English-centered, east-to-west account of early America.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011 interview explains the particular resource; Parmenter1999 p124 separately identifies White alongside James Axtell and James Merrell in New Worlds for All. Their credit remains plural. Bailyn1995 also names White’s resource in Calloway’s Revolution book. These are distinct witnesses, consolidated in one contribution claim. The complete books and Calloway’s1992 review remain unread.
primary_locators: Five Books section5 The Middle Ground, both answers; Jon W. Parmenter1999 p124 opening paragraph; Bailyn1995 paragraph beginning Further, following the lead.
